passage:
Mentor's note, new-joiner programme, Friday.
Vaibhav has been keen to meet people on other teams. This morning he wanted to ask Madhav from finance about the budget tool. I saw him walk toward Madhav's desk, then stop. Madhav had his earphones in, was typing fast, and had two coffee cups beside him, clearly racing a deadline. Vaibhav turned back and sat down.
At lunch, Madhav was sitting alone, earphones off, stretching. Vaibhav went over. "Hi, I'm Vaibhav, new in operations. Do you have five minutes sometime about the budget tool?" Madhav smiled. "Sit, I've got ten now. This morning was madness." They talked for twenty minutes.
Afterwards I mentioned to Vaibhav that waiting was a good call. He said he didn't want to be the person who interrupts.

qa.q: What did Madhav have beside him at his desk?
qa.a: Two coffee cups.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he stopped near Madhav's desk?
qa.a: He was hesitant and considerate, sensing from the earphones and fast typing that Madhav was under pressure, and didn't want to intrude.

qa.q: Why did waiting until lunch work better?
qa.a: Madhav was relaxed and free, so he welcomed the question warmly and even gave more time than asked.

qa.q: How might Madhav have reacted if Vaibhav had interrupted in the morning?
qa.a: He might have felt annoyed or rushed and given a short answer, making a worse first impression.

grounding: Shows a person noticing cues that someone is busy and holding off on starting a chat, which leads to a warmer reply later.

passage:
Tuesday night.
I've been meaning to ask Kishore from 4B about the society meeting on water tanks. Today I saw him at the gate. He was on the phone, frowning, carrying three bags of groceries, walking fast. I almost said "Hi, one quick thing." Then I noticed he didn't even look up. So I just nodded and let him pass.
Tomorrow, I thought.
This evening I saw him again on the bench outside, feeding the cats, relaxed. I sat down and asked about the meeting. He laughed. "Thank god you didn't catch me this morning. My mother's flight was delayed and I was going mad." He told me everything about the tanks and even offered to come with me to the next meeting.
Glad I waited.
Kiran

qa.q: What was Kishore carrying at the gate?
qa.a: Three bags of groceries.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel on deciding to let Kishore pass?
qa.a: Kiran felt a little hesitant but considerate, sensing from his frown and hurry that it wasn't the right moment.

qa.q: What did Kiran's choice to wait lead to?
qa.a: A relaxed, warm conversation in the evening where Kishore shared everything and offered to come to the next meeting.

qa.q: How was Kishore feeling that morning?
qa.a: He was stressed and distracted because his mother's flight was delayed.

grounding: Shows a person reading cues that a neighbour is hurried and turned away, holding off, and getting a warm reply later.

passage:
Conference volunteer's note, day two, lunch break.
I noticed a young delegate, Mahima, sitting alone at the end of a long table, looking at her phone but not scrolling. Around her, groups were laughing. A young man with a name badge, Tarun, came over with his plate. "Hi, is this seat free? I don't know anyone here either."
Mahima looked up. Her shoulders stiffened for a second, and she glanced around as if checking. Then she smiled. "Yes, please. I'm Mahima, from Indore. Which session did you come for?" Tarun lit up. They talked through the whole lunch, and I later saw them sitting together in the afternoon session.
I've suggested to the organisers that we add a "sit anywhere" table tomorrow for people who come alone.

qa.q: What did Tarun say when he came over?
qa.a: He said, 'Hi, is this seat free? I don't know anyone here either.'

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when Tarun first spoke to her?
qa.a: She felt both wary and relieved, stiffening and glancing around before smiling and welcoming him.

qa.q: What did Mahima's reply do well?
qa.a: She answered warmly and asked a question back, which rewarded Tarun for taking the risk and started a real conversation.

qa.q: How did Tarun seem to feel after Mahima's question?
qa.a: He lit up, relieved and pleased that his approach was welcomed.

grounding: Shows a person sitting alone who feels wary and relieved when approached, and rewards the stranger with a warm reply and a question back.

passage:
Saturday, Hyderabad, week three.
I was sitting alone on a bench at the lake, feeling homesick for Lucknow, when a woman about my age sat at the other end. After a minute she said, "Sorry to bother you. Do you come here often? I just moved here and don't know anyone."
My first thought was: what does she want? My second thought was: oh, thank god, a person.
I said, "I just moved too! Three weeks ago. I'm Ayesha. Where are you from?" She said, "Sudha, from Madurai." We talked about the terrible autos and the good biryani and our landladies.
She said, "I almost didn't say anything." I said, "I'm so glad you did."
We're meeting at the same bench next Saturday.
Ayesha

qa.a: Three weeks ago.

qa.a: She said she almost didn't say anything, so she was nervous but glad it went well.

Kindergarten note, Monday.
During free play, Harsha (5) was telling Minakshi about her new cat: "And she has white socks and she sleeps on my—" Then the bubble machine started in the corner, and Harsha ran off mid-sentence. Minakshi stood there, looking puzzled and a bit sad.

I'll practise "bye, I'm going now" with the whole class this week.

Sunday night
Nanaji called at five and I talked for FORTY minutes. I wanted to go and play cricket with my cousin Amandeep, who was waiting at the door with the bat. But every time I tried to stop, Nanaji asked another question, and I didn't know how to say bye without being rude. So I kept telling him about school, then about my science project, then about the cat.
Amandeep finally took the phone and said, "Okay Nanaji, Yash has to go now. We'll call again tomorrow! Love you, bye!" Nanaji laughed and said bye.
It was so easy! I wrote it down: "Okay, I need to go now. Talk tomorrow. Love you, bye!"
Next time I'll use it.
Yash

qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Yash feel during the call?

passage: In their village above Gangtok, Pema, ten, sat on the steps with the phone pressed to her ear. Mola, her grandmother in town, had been talking for half an hour. Pema had told her about school, the new goat, and the rain. Now her tea was cold and her homework was waiting. But every time Mola paused, Pema said "Mm" and Mola started a new story. Her brother Ojas watched from the doorway. When Mola paused again, Ojas whispered, "Say: 'Okay Mola, I have to do homework now. I'll call on Sunday. Love you!'" Pema hesitated, then said it. Mola laughed. "Of course, go study! Sunday, then." Pema hung up, surprised. "She didn't mind at all!" Ojas grinned. "She just needed a signal."

qa.a: Pema felt stuck and a bit restless, with cold tea and homework waiting, unsure how to end the call.

qa.a: It gave a clear signal, a reason, a plan to call again and a warm 'Love you', so Mola didn't feel cut off.

qa.a: Mola didn't mind at all, laughing and agreeing to talk on Sunday.

passage: In his Madrid flat, Javier, nine, was on a video call with his abuelo in Seville. It had been going for ages. His friend Jamal was waiting in the hallway with a football, making faces. The call ended. Javier looked at Mamá. "That was it?" "That was it." Javier ran out, relieved, but he also remembered to call the next day.

passage:
At Sangeeta's birthday party last month, I got stuck near the balcony with her, talking about the college canteen. It was a nice chat, but I was starving and the biryani was disappearing.
Earlier that evening, I'd seen someone just walk away from a person mid-sentence, and that person looked hurt. I didn't want to do that.
So when there was a natural pause, I smiled and said, "It was really great talking about this. I'm off to get some food before it's gone. Catch you later?" Sangeeta laughed. "Go, go! Save me a kebab." I brought her one, actually.
The next week she messaged me first, asking if I wanted to join her study group. I think that small, warm exit mattered more than I realised. I'm Deepak, by the way, still bad at parties but getting better.

qa.q: What was disappearing at the party?
qa.a: The biryani.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling before leaving the conversation?
qa.a: Deepak was hungry and a little worried about leaving rudely, having seen someone look hurt after an abrupt exit.

qa.q: What made Deepak's exit graceful?
qa.a: Deepak waited for a pause, said it was great talking, named the reason for leaving and added 'Catch you later?', keeping it warm.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta respond to the exit?
qa.a: She laughed, asked for a kebab and later messaged Deepak first, showing she felt good about the chat.

grounding: Shows a student at a party leaving a conversation with a clear, positive closing that keeps the door open.

I watched Bhupen, a first-year, doing something many students find hard. He'd been chatting with Vasudha from the second year for about fifteen minutes near the tea counter. I could see he wanted to meet the others from his course, who were waving at him.
He waited for a pause and said, "Vasudha, this was really great. I'm going to say hi to my course people, but let's talk again at the library?" She smiled and said, "Definitely." He left warmly, and she went back to her friends looking pleased.
Later I saw them sitting together at breakfast. I'll mention this at the next freshers' talk as a good example of ending a conversation well.

passage:

Cousin's engagement party. Trisha, my cousin's friend, found me by the dessert table and talked for a long time about her law exams. She's lovely! But my feet hurt and Mummy was signalling me to help with the gifts.
I used to just mumble "okay, bye" and vanish. Tonight I tried something new. When Trisha paused, I said, "It was so nice talking to you, I really hope the exams go well. I have to go help Mummy with the gifts now, but let's catch up at the wedding?" Trisha said, "Yes! Save me a seat!"

Sarita

passage: In the office break room, Vikas was halfway through explaining his idea for the new client report to Chaitanya. passage:
Subject: Our chat yesterday

Hi Sabina,

I wanted to say thanks for your message last night. Honestly, when you glanced at your phone and said "gotta run" while I was halfway through telling you about the vendor problem, I felt a bit brushed off. I went back to my desk thinking maybe I'd been boring you.

Then your text came: "Sorry, got called into a meeting, I really want to hear the rest. Tomorrow at 10?" That made a huge difference. I didn't feel dismissed anymore.

So see you at 10. I'll bring the numbers.

And for what it's worth, I've started doing the same thing when I have to rush off. It's a small habit, but it helps.

Manoj

passage:
Dear Kiran,

You asked how I handle Lalremsiami aunty downstairs, who talks for an hour every time I pass her door. I love her, but I also have work.

Here's what I tried yesterday. She was telling me about her nephew's wedding, the caterer, the band, the cousin who fell into the flowers. When she took a breath, I said, "So the wedding was beautiful, and the band was late, and your cousin survived the flowers! Thank you for telling me, aunty. I have to get to the office now, but I want to hear the photos part on Sunday."

She laughed and patted my arm. "Go, go, beta." No hurt feelings at all.

Summarise, thank, then name what you have to do. It works.

Chaitanya

qa.a: Into the flowers.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling while Lalremsiami aunty talked?

qa.q: Which steps made Chaitanya's ending kind and clear?
qa.a: Summarising her story, thanking her, naming the need to go to the office and promising to hear more on Sunday.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami aunty respond to the ending?
qa.a: She laughed and patted Chaitanya's arm, with no hurt feelings.

grounding: Shows a listener gently interrupting a long talker with a summary and thanks, then naming what they must do next.

"So, the question was about workplace habits? Okay. I'm Sharmila, I work in HR, and I'll tell you about Rashmi.

passage:
Monday: At the park, Noor, two, went on the swing, fell off gently, cried, and then got ice cream.
Tuesday: Manjula showed her a photo of the swing. Noor pointed. "Swing! Up!" Manjula said, "Yes, you went up high!"
Friday: Looking at the photo again, Noor said, "Swing. Up. Fall. Cry. Ice cream!" Manjula laughed. "You fell, you cried, and then we had ice cream!" Noor nodded hard. "Ice cream!"

qa.q: What did Noor get after falling off the swing?
qa.a: Ice cream.

qa.q: How did Noor seem to feel on Friday, retelling the story?
qa.a: She seemed proud and excited, nodding hard and shouting 'Ice cream!'

qa.q: How did Manjula help Noor's retelling grow?
qa.a: She echoed Noor's words each time, turning fragments into a full sentence and helping her remember the sequence.

qa.q: What changed between Tuesday and Friday?
qa.a: On Tuesday Noor said two words; by Friday she told a five-part sequence of what happened.

grounding: Shows a toddler recounting a park trip in fragments that grow over days, as an adult echoes them.

passage: In their Pune flat, Noor, two and a half, pulled her father Chetan to the fridge, where a drawing from the park was stuck. "Papa! Doggy! Run!" Chetan crouched. "The doggy ran at the park?" "Doggy run. Ball. Noor throw!" "You threw the ball, and the doggy ran after it!" Noor jumped up and down. "Doggy bring back!" "Yes! The doggy brought it back to you." Noor beamed and told it again.

qa.q: What was stuck on the fridge?
qa.a: A drawing from the park.

qa.q: What does Noor jumping up and down suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was excited and happy, proud to tell her story.

qa.q: How did Chetan's echoes help Noor?
qa.a: He turned her fragments into full sentences, which builds her language and memory of the park.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel when Noor tells it again?
qa.a: He probably feels delighted and proud of her growing words.

grounding: Shows a toddler recounting a park trip in fragments and a parent echoing them to build language and memory.

passage:
Monday: Deepak, five, ran in from the colony gate. "Mummy! I saw a dog as big as a bus! It had three tails!" Neelam laughed. "Three tails! What colour?" "Purple!" "Wow, what a story!"
Wednesday: At dinner, Deepak said, "I flew to school today. Over the trees." Neelam smiled. "Was that in your dream or for real?" Deepak thought. "Dream. But it felt real!" "Dreams can feel very real."
Saturday: Deepak said, "I saw a big dog." Then he added, "A pretend one, a bus dog!" Neelam hugged him, laughing. "I love your pretend dogs."

qa.q: How many tails did Deepak say the dog had?
qa.a: Three tails.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel telling his tall tales?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud of his imaginative stories.

qa.q: How did Neelam keep a gentle line on facts?
qa.a: She enjoyed the stories but asked 'Was that in your dream or for real?', helping Deepak separate pretend from real.

qa.q: What changed in Deepak by Saturday?
qa.a: He started labelling his own tall tale as 'a pretend one' without being asked.

grounding: Shows a child telling exaggerated tales and a parent enjoying them while gently separating pretend from real.

passage: During the power cut at the preschool, the fans stopped, and Neelam ma'am gathered the children in the corridor with a torch for story time. Rukmini, five, put her hand up. "I saw a tiger in my garden! It was THIS big!" She spread her arms. "It ate my slipper!" The children gasped. Neelam ma'am smiled. "A tiger! That's a big story. Was it a real tiger or a pretend tiger?" Rukmini thought. "Pretend. But it was hungry." Everyone laughed. "Pretend tigers get very hungry," Neelam ma'am said. "Shall we make up more of its story?" The class spent the power cut deciding what the tiger ate next.

qa.q: What did Rukmini say the tiger ate?
qa.a: Her slipper.

qa.q: How did Rukmini seem to feel telling the tiger story?
qa.a: She seemed excited and proud, spreading her arms to show its size.

qa.q: What did Neelam ma'am do that respected both imagination and facts?
qa.a: She enjoyed the story but asked if it was real or pretend, then turned it into a shared make-believe game.

qa.q: How did the other children respond to Rukmini's story?
qa.a: They gasped and then laughed, joining in to invent more of the tiger's story.

grounding: Shows a child telling a tall tale and an adult enjoying it while gently marking the line between pretend and real.

passage: At the colony pool in Chennai, Jaya, six, climbed out dripping and ran to her big sister Aditi. "Akka! I swam with a whale! A real whale! It had a hat!" Aditi raised her eyebrows. "A whale in the colony pool?" "Yes! It said hello!" Aditi laughed. "That's an amazing story. Was it real, or a pretend whale?" Jaya giggled. "Pretend. But it had a hat." "The best whales have hats," Aditi said. "Tell me what colour the hat was." Jaya told her, all the way home.

qa.q: What did Jaya say the whale had?
qa.a: A hat.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel telling her whale story?
qa.a: She felt excited and happy, giggling as she told it.

qa.q: How did Aditi keep a gentle line on facts?
qa.a: She asked if it was real or pretend, then kept enjoying the story, asking about the hat.

qa.q: What would change if Aditi had called it a lie?
qa.a: Jaya might have felt ashamed and stopped sharing her imaginative stories.

grounding: Shows a child telling a tall tale and an older sister enjoying it while gently marking what is pretend.

passage: Every Sunday at Gogo's house in Soweto, Thabo, ten, heard the same story. When Grandpa was young, he had walked forty kilometres to his first job with only one pair of shoes, carrying them in his hands so they wouldn't wear out. Thabo's cousin Gabriel rolled his eyes. "We know, Gogo." But Thabo never minded. He liked hearing how Grandpa put the shoes on only at the factory gate. At school, when a teacher asked the class to write about someone they admired, Thabo wrote about Grandpa's shoes. He read it aloud. His voice shook a little at the end. That evening, he told Gogo about it. She squeezed his hand. "You carry him too, now." Thabo felt taller all week.

qa.q: How far did Grandpa walk to his first job?
qa.a: Forty kilometres.

qa.q: How did Thabo feel after Gogo said 'You carry him too, now'?
qa.a: He felt proud and connected, feeling taller all week.

qa.q: How could a teacher use Thabo's story to help other children?
qa.a: The teacher could invite others to share a family story, helping them feel a sense of belonging too.

qa.q: How does Gabriel see the repeated story?
qa.a: Gabriel seems bored by it, rolling his eyes, while Thabo finds it meaningful.

grounding: Shows a child who repeatedly hears a family story about his grandfather and gains a sense of place and belonging.

passage: For the Class 4 project "My Family Story," Santosh stood at the front of the room holding a photo. "I was born during the big floods," he said. "The water came up to the second floor. My mother was in the hospital, and our neighbours carried food to her in a boat made of plastic drums." The class went quiet. Raghav, in the front row, whispered, "Really?" Santosh nodded. "My father tells it every year on my birthday. He says that's why our building is my family too." The teacher asked how that made him feel. Santosh thought. "Like I belong to a lot of people." When he sat down, Raghav leaned over. "My dad has a story about a train. I'll tell you at lunch."

qa.q: How did the neighbours carry food to Santosh's mother?
qa.a: In a boat made of plastic drums.

qa.q: How does Santosh feel about his birth story?
qa.a: He feels proud and connected, like he belongs to a lot of people.

qa.q: How could the teacher build on this project?
qa.a: The teacher could invite each child to share a family story, as Raghav wants to, so everyone feels a sense of belonging.

qa.q: How did Raghav respond to Santosh's story?
qa.a: He was amazed, whispering 'Really?', and wanted to share his own family story at lunch.

grounding: Shows a child who has heard his birth story many times, which gives him a sense of place and belonging.

passage:
Diwali: At Paati Chandrika's house, Shankar, nine, heard the story again. How Thatha started his cycle repair shop with one borrowed spanner, and fixed a doctor's cycle so well the doctor sent the whole street.
A month later: At school, when a boy teased him about his old cycle, Shankar said, "My Thatha fixed cycles for the whole street. This one is special." He didn't feel small at all.
Pongal: Shankar sat next to Paati and said, "Tell the spanner story again." Then, halfway through, he told it himself, with every detail. Paati laughed and wiped her eyes. "Now it's your story too."

qa.q: What did Thatha start his shop with?
qa.a: One borrowed spanner.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when the boy teased him?
qa.a: He didn't feel small at all; he felt proud and confident because of Thatha's story.

qa.q: What would you advise a family that wants children to feel they belong?
qa.a: Tell family stories often, and let children retell them, like Shankar did at Pongal.

qa.q: How did Paati feel when Shankar told the story himself?
qa.a: She was moved and happy, laughing and wiping her eyes.

grounding: Shows a child hearing a family story repeatedly, which gives him pride, a place and a sense of belonging.
